compensating.new: final int value = StringUtils.decodeInt(str); if (value != 0 && (value < 0) != (str.charAt(0) == '-')) { throw new NumberFormatException("For input string: \"" + str + "\""); } return Integer.valueOf(value);
compensating.why: hop 1 rejects a decoded value whose sign disagrees with the sign of the string
hop 4 also rejects more than ten digits
hop 1 also rejects a string longer than the longest int literal

ownership_reason: Only the gold holds the running value together with the next digit, the radix and the sign, which is what the per-digit range decision needs; hops 1-4 read the zero length case, the sign, the radix prefix and the empty digit string, and get back one int, in which a value that wrapped around cannot be told apart from a value in range (2147483648 comes back as -2147483648; "10" + Long.MAX_VALUE comes back as the positive 1661992959, so not even the sign betrays it). The convention is pinned outside the gold: NumberUtils.createNumber, the production caller of the facade, tries successively larger types from Integer to BigInteger and widens to createLong only when createInteger throws NumberFormatException (its 'L' branch takes the same step one size up, 'Too big for a long'); Fraction.getFraction(String) converts a whole number with Integer.parseInt and rejects 2147483648 as too big (FractionTest testFactory_String_double, passing); NumberUtils.createLong converts with Long.valueOf, the same rule for long. The gold's javadoc promises the value of the number, which -2147483648 is not for the digits 2147483648. A pre-check of the digits with another parser at hop 3 or 4 (Long.parseLong or BigInteger) passes the existing tests but is a second implementation of the gold's decision; a length limit of ten digits passes them too but rejects valid ints such as 2147483647; a comparison of the decimal digit string with "2147483647" at hop 3 passes them but leaves hex and octal values wrapping around (createInteger("0x80000000") = -2147483648).
